nameStory: Cotton Deergrass gets its name from the fluffy white bristles that emerge from its flowers, looking just like tiny tufts of cotton on a stick. The 'deergrass' part comes from the traditional belief that deer and other wildlife browse on sedges like this one, though the connection is more about the family than this specific diminutive species.
description: Cotton Deergrass is a small, unassuming member of the sedge family that packs a visual punch when it blooms. This petite plant grows only about 16 inches tall at most, producing slender stems from underground runners called rhizomes. What makes it special are the cloud-like white bristles that emerge from tiny flower clusters, creating cotton-ball effects that seem almost magical in their bog and meadow homes. Despite its delicate appearance, this tough little sedge thrives in some of New England's most challenging wetland environments.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: The star feature - cottony white bristles that extend nearly an inch beyond the tiny flower spikelet, creating fluffy white tufts that feel soft and silky when gently touched

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Extremely short leaves, less than half an inch long, that are easy to overlook - they feel thin and grass-like but are much shorter than you'd expect

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing sedge reaching only 16 inches tall, forming small clumps connected by underground runners rather than dense tufts

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender, triangular stems typical of sedges - roll them between your fingers and you'll feel the characteristic three-sided shape

habitat: Look for Cotton Deergrass in New England's coldest, most pristine wetlands - especially sphagnum bogs and calcium-rich mountain meadows at higher elevations. It thrives in the acidic, nutrient-poor conditions of bogs alongside cranberries and pitcher plants, as well as in alkaline seeps and fens in mountainous areas. This is a plant of the region's most specialized and often remote wetland habitats.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as the snow melts, with fresh green shoots appearing from the underground rhizomes in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time when the distinctive white cotton-like bristles are fully developed and most visible, typically in mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: The cottony bristles begin to disperse seeds and may become less prominent, while the plant starts to senesce for winter.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to underground rhizomes, leaving little trace above ground in the frozen bog landscape.

funFact: Despite being called 'alpine' in its scientific name, Cotton Deergrass has one of the widest distributions of any plant on Earth - it grows in suitable habitats all the way around the northern hemisphere, from New England bogs to Siberian tundra to Scandinavian fens!
confusionNotes: The cottony white bristles make this nearly impossible to confuse with anything else when in bloom - no other small sedge in New England produces such prominent fluffy white tufts. When not flowering, it's just another tiny, unremarkable sedge that's easily overlooked.
contextualKnowledge: Like many sedges, Cotton Deergrass is often overlooked by casual observers who might dismiss it as 'just grass,' but sedges are actually more closely related to rushes than to true grasses and have their own fascinating ecology in wetland communities.
compareHints: Among its Trichophorum relatives, Cotton Deergrass is distinguished by its extremely short leaves and prominent white bristles. Tufted Bulrush forms denser clumps, while Bashful and Clinton's Bulrushes have longer, more prominent leaves and less showy bristles. The cotton-like bristles extending well beyond the flower cluster are Cotton Deergrass's signature feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Tufted bulrush differs from its Trichophorum relatives by its distinctive cushion-forming growth habit – cotton deergrass grows in loose colonies rather than tight tufts, while bashful bulrush has broader leaves and a more upright stance.

Bashful Bulrush is much smaller and more delicate than its Trichophorum relatives - while Tufted Bulrush forms dense, robust clumps and Cotton Deergrass has distinctive white, fluffy seed heads, Bashful Bulrush stays low and inconspicuous.
Clinton's Bulrush differs from its relative Tufted Bulrush by forming denser clumps and lacking the cottony bristles that other deergrasses often have.
